1.explanation: The bug arises because prepareFrame always calls imageSource.getImage with the map’s display pixelRatio, even if the source is configured to load images at a different pixel ratio (e.g. hidpi = false). Then renderFrame unconditionally sizes the HTMLCanvasElement to frameState.pixelRatio × viewport size rather than the image’s own pixelRatio. As a result, when the image itself is only 1× resolution but the canvas is created at 2×, the canvas buffer is 4× larger than needed. Fixing requires switching both the getImage() call in prepareFrame and the canvas.width/height calculation in renderFrame to use the image’s pixelRatio (this.image_.getPixelRatio()) instead of frameState.pixelRatio when the source’s pixel ratio differs.
1.bug_scenario: On HiDPI displays (e.g. pixelRatio = 2) using a WMS image source configured with hidpi = false (so the source image is fetched at pixelRatio = 1), the canvas renderer still allocates a canvas at display pixelRatio (2× width and height), i.e. 4× the area (and memory) needed to draw the 1× image. The screenshots show a canvas element twice as large as the requested image.

2.explanation: The bug lives in CanvasImageLayerRenderer. In renderFrame(), the canvas dimensions are set using the device pixelRatio (frameState.pixelRatio) rather than the image’s pixel ratio (image.getPixelRatio()). As a result, when the source image has pixelRatio = 1 on a HiDPI display, the canvas is unnecessarily large. Adjusting canvas.width and canvas.height to use image.getPixelRatio() instead of frameState.pixelRatio will correct the memory over‐allocation.
2.bug_scenario: On high‐DPI (e.g. Retina) displays, image layers loaded from sources such as WMS (which often have pixelRatio = 1) are being rendered to canvases sized according to the device pixelRatio (e.g. 2). The code in CanvasImageLayerRenderer always sets canvas.width and .height based on frameState.pixelRatio, not the image’s own pixelRatio. When image.getPixelRatio() = 1 but device pixelRatio = 2, the canvas ends up twice as wide/tall as needed, consuming 4× the memory.
